en.title: The Diplomat's Devil's Waltz: Composer Marcelo Zarvos on Crafting the Wylers' Sound
en.summary: The intricate dance of power and passion in Netflix's **The Diplomat** finds its voice in the masterful score by **Marcelo Zarvos**. He reveals the unique inspirations behind the Wylers' captivating musical themes.
en.body:
Netflix's **The Diplomat** isn't just a political thriller; it's a high-stakes performance, a meticulously choreographed dance between **Keri Russell**'s Kate Wyler and **Rufus Sewell**'s Hal Wyler. Composer **Marcelo Zarvos**, known for his work on **Ray Donovan** and **Fences**, sees this dynamic as central to his scoring approach. He recently shared that the show's blend of personal and political maneuvering often felt like a dance, a perfect metaphor for the Wylers themselves, who are constantly performing for the world stage. Zarvos’ ability to capture the contradictions and strengths of these richly drawn characters has been key to the series' sonic identity.

When approaching **The Diplomat**, Zarvos revisited his early work on **The Good Shepherd**, noting a shared DNA in political intrigue and maneuvering. However, he quickly distinguished the two projects. Unlike the more pervasive score of **The Good Shepherd**, music in **The Diplomat** is used with striking economy, appearing sparingly and with specific intent. Furthermore, the distinct sense of humor woven into the series sets it apart. "There was something in the DNA of those scores," Zarvos stated, reflecting on his past work. "Ultimately, at first, I thought, oh, it's going to be just like The Good Shepherd. But of course, a big difference with The Diplomat is, first, how the music is used very sparingly and specifically; it's the opposite of wall-to-wall music in The Diplomat. Also, there's humor in it that's a little bit different than The Good Shepherd." He further elaborated on the desired tone, recalling conversations about a "confidence and leanness" in the score, echoing a less-is-more philosophy he'd encountered previously.

## The Wylers' "Devil's Waltz"

Fans have been captivated by the complex relationship between Kate and Hal, a dynamic that Zarvos translates into music with remarkable precision. The composer’s work on **The Diplomat** Season 2, which premiered on October 31, 2024, continues to explore these intricate themes. His scoring style, characterized by layered motifs and emotive undertones, provides a rich sonic tapestry for the show's dramatic highs and personal lows. Zarvos' previous collaborations with director **Debora Cahn** have clearly established a strong creative rapport, allowing him to deeply understand and translate the nuances of the narrative into music. The specific piece often referred to as the "Devil's Waltz" encapsulates the volatile yet compelling nature of the Wylers' marriage, a perfect storm of ambition, affection, and political gamesmanship.

## Fan Response to the Score

The music of **The Diplomat** has undoubtedly become a character in itself, enhancing the tension and emotional resonance for viewers. The deliberate use of score allows key moments to land with greater impact, and **Marcelo Zarvos**' thematic contributions are frequently highlighted by fans discussing the series online. The way the score underscores the Wylers' often volatile interactions, shifting from moments of subtle understanding to outright conflict, has been a particular point of praise, demonstrating how effectively Zarvos captures the show's unique tone and the complexities of its central relationship.

## What's Next

As **The Diplomat** continues to navigate international crises and personal entanglements, **Marcelo Zarvos**' score will undoubtedly remain a crucial element in amplifying the drama. Fans can anticipate further exploration of the Wylers' evolving dynamic through Zarvos' distinctive musical voice in potential future seasons.

The Wylers, played by Keri Russell and Rufus Sewell, are often performers.  They are two of the best characters on television at the moment. The richly drawn characters, with all their contradictions and strengths, provide plenty of inspiration for Zarvos. He is the composer behind Fences , Enough Said , Wonder , Nonnas , and Ray Donovan , not to mention KPop Demon Hunters . Recently, the composer spoke with What’s On Netflix about his approach to scoring the highs and lows of the Wyler couple in The Diplomat . When you started The Diplomat , did you think about one of your earliest scoring jobs, The Good Shepherd , when approaching the show’s political intrigue and maneuvering? I really did think about it. There was something in the DNA of those scores. Ultimately, at first, I thought, oh, it’s going to be just like The Good Shepherd . But of course, a big difference with The Diplomat is, first, how the music is used very sparingly and specifically; it’s the opposite of wall-to-wall music in The Diplomat . Also, there’s humor in it that’s a little bit different than The Good Shepherd .  But I thought about it, and some of the things that they were looking for, they talked a lot about this kind of confidence and leanness in the score. And I remember talking to Robert De Niro when I was doing The Good Shepherd , and he really… It was a less-is-more approach. But it was a movie, and there was a lot more score. Certainly, my experience in writing for The Good Shepherd informed my writing for The Diplomat . What were your early impressions of the Wylers? What themes, cues, and motifs did you establish that you still return to? There was a lot of talk about a lot of waltzes. I always think that in those settings, there’s a real formality to those settings, and I thought immediately of European court dances, waltzes, minuets, things that were light marches and things like that, all the way to really heavy, also the light version and the super-heavy version.  Then Deb would sometimes talk about almost like the devil’s waltz. Sometimes there’s devilish things going on with the shenanigans of the Foreign Service, all the intrigue and some of the sabotage. It was courtly dances, but not just the gentle kinds, sometimes the mean and a little bit shocking. There are things that happen in the show throughout, and certainly all the way, including the last season, that are very big things. The writing is a big part of the show’s appeal. The stakes are both personal and global. How much does that give you to work with as a composer?
